newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU groups criticise slow postal liberalisation.
newsitem.headline: EU groups criticise slow postal liberalisation.

text.p: Express and direct mail operators, advertisers, publishers and other industry groups on Wednesday criticised a decision by European Union post ministers to delay significant liberalisation of postal services until at least 2003.
"The delay to liberalisation is a major blow to the growth of cross-frontier business in the single market," the Postal Users Group (PUG) said in a statement.
EU ministers agreed on Wednesday a plan for opening up competition in the postal sector which would remove state monopolies over only about two percent of EU mail in an initial stage.
They set a target date of 2003 for removing state monopolies over direct, or "junk", mail and cross-border mail. The formal decision whether to open up those sectors would be made before 2000.

PUG, which represents advertisers, publishers, the direct mail industry and other groups, said it expected that postal users and carriers would now file a barrage of unfair competition complaints to the European Commission about state postal monopolies.

Both PUG and the European Express Organisation (EEO) said they were looking forward to a notice the Commission planned to publish at the beginning of the year on how it will apply EU competition rules to the postal sector.
The EEO represents express mail operators such as United Parcel Service, Federal Express and Deutsche Paket Dienst.

EEO secretary-general Anton van der Lande said the EEO wanted the Commission to take a strong line on cross-subsidies -- the use by state post offices of profits from their monopoly services to prop up their express mail operations.

Given the ministers' decision to move slowly to chip away at postal monopolies, "a notice ensuring that the (EU treaty) competition rules do also apply to the postal sector is even more necessary," he told Reuters.
He said express operators would take their case to the European Court of Justice if necessary.

The European Magazine Publishers Federation said EU legislation on postal service must compensate for the slow liberalisation by better addressing issues such as quality of service and transparency of accounting practices.
"As postal operators have now been granted very wide powers for monopolising sectors of mail, it becomes imperative that the directive strike a balance in other areas," it said in a statement.
"Although not in the public sector millions of jobs in the press, direct marketing and mail order are dependent on efficient and reliable postal services to survive."
